en: Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga Pācittiyakaṇḍa
Surāpānavagga 56.
The Training Rule on Jotika.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying among the Bhaggas at Susumāragira, in the Bhesakaḷā Grove, in the Deer Park.
Now at that time, during the winter season, some monks had kindled a fire using a large hollow log and were warming themselves.
A black snake, heated by the fire, emerged from that hollow and threw the monks down.
The monks ran hither and thither.
Those monks who were of few desires... they complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying:
"How can these monks, having kindled a fire, warm themselves? ... [The Buddha asked:
"Is it true, monks, that monks, having kindled a fire, warm themselves?"
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:

“… How can those foolish men, monks, having kindled a fire, dry themselves by its heat? This is not suitable for you, monks, this is not becoming, this is not fitting, this is not worthy of a recluse, this is not proper, and it is not to be done.”
“Monks, this does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule as follows:
‘Should any monk, desiring to warm himself, kindle a fire or cause one to be kindled, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).’”
Thus this training rule was laid down by the Blessed One for the monks.
Now at that time, the monks were ill.
The monks who were visiting the sick said this to the sick monks:
“Is it bearable, friend? Are you getting by?
“In the past, friends, we would kindle a fire and warm ourselves;
by that we were at ease.”
"But now, fearing that it has been forbidden by the Blessed One, we do not warm ourselves; because of that, we have no comfort.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One... [the Buddha said:
"I allow you, monks, for a sick monk, having kindled a fire himself or having had one kindled, to warm himself."
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule thus:
"Whosoever monk, not being ill, desiring to warm himself, should kindle a fire or cause one to be kindled, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
In this way, this training rule was laid down by the Blessed One for the monks.
Now at that time, the monks were anxious about using lamps, torches, and saunas.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One...
[as before] ... "I allow you, monks, on such an occasion, to kindle a fire and have one kindled."
And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule:
“Whosoever, being not ill, should kindle a fire or have one kindled for the purpose of warming himself, except when there is a suitable reason, that is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
Whosoever, moreover:
Whoever is such a one … [as described] … “a bhikkhu” … [and so on] … this is the meaning intended here by the term “bhikkhu.”
"One who is not ill" means one for whom there is comfort without fire.
"One who is ill" means...
One for whom there is no comfort without fire.
"Desiring to warm oneself" means wishing to heat it.
"Light" (joti) is a term for fire.
"One should kindle" means...
If she kindles it herself, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
"Causes to be kindled" means if she commands another to do so, there is an offense of expiation.
If, having been instructed once, he kindles even a great deal [of fire], there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya),
except in the case of such a reason;
"except in the case of such a reason" means excluding such a reason.

If one who is not ill, perceiving himself as not ill, kindles a fire or causes it to be kindled for the purpose of warming himself, except when there is a suitable reason, he commits an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
If one who is not ill, being doubtful, kindles a fire or causes it to be kindled for the purpose of warming himself, except when there is a suitable reason, he commits an offense entailing expiation.

If one who is not ill, perceiving himself as ill, kindles a fire or causes it to be kindled for the purpose of warming himself, except when there is a suitable reason, he commits an offense entailing expiation.
If he tosses it back, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If he is ill but perceives himself as not ill, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If he is ill but is uncertain of it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If one is ill and perceives oneself as ill, there is no offense.
There is no offense for one who is ill.
He dries himself with what has been prepared by another;
he dries himself with charcoal that has been extinguished;
or he does so by means of a lamp, a torch, or a sauna, for such purposes.
In times of distress,
for one who is insane,
and for the first offender.
The sixth training rule concerning Jotika is finished.
